A few important requirements to understand before submitting your proposal.




Who is eligible to contribute?

EPCL welcomes criminal justice practitioners, researchers, academic faculty, undergraduate and graduate students, administrators, policymakers, retired professionals, and other individuals with relevant knowledge or experience.
Institutional affiliation, academic credentials, and previous publication experience are not prerequisites.



Originality and intellectual property

Contributions should represent original work and must not infringe upon the intellectual property rights of others.
Contributors are responsible for appropriately acknowledging sources. Previously published material, manuscripts under consideration elsewhere, and substantially overlapping submissions must be disclosed.



Professional and ethical standards

Contributors must:

Properly attribute sources and intellectual contributions.
Disclose relevant conflicts of interest.
Identify applicable funding and material support.
Obtain permissions for copyrighted materials.
Protect confidential and personally identifiable information.
Obtain appropriate authorization for research involving human participants when required.

EPCL may request clarification regarding research ethics, institutional approvals, or data permissions.



Manuscript formatting requirements

EPCL accepts proposals across three contribution categories. Contributors should select the category that most closely reflects the purpose and format of their proposed work.


Communicating research and expanding professional knowledge.
This category is intended for contributions that explain, evaluate, synthesize, or communicate research and established knowledge.
Examples include:

Original research articles
Literature reviews
Research summaries
Educational explainers
Program and policy evaluations
Evidence-based practice reviews
Methodological discussions

Contributions should clearly communicate their evidence base and explain the relevance of their findings or subject matter to criminal justice professionals and researchers.



Examining ideas, challenging assumptions, and encouraging professional discussion.
This category provides a platform for examining contemporary issues, discussing competing perspectives, and advancing informed professional dialogue.
Examples include:

Policy analyses
Professional commentary
Opinion essays grounded in evidence
Ethical discussions
Emerging issues in criminal justice
Institutional and organizational critiques
Debates concerning professional practice

Contributions should present a coherent argument, engage meaningfully with relevant evidence or experience, and encourage constructive discussion.



Sharing professional knowledge and practical experience.
This category is intended for practitioners and professionals interested in communicating experiences, describing initiatives, and sharing lessons from the field.
Examples include:

Case studies
Descriptions of innovative practices
Implementation experiences
Lessons learned from professional practice
Interviews with criminal justice professionals
Operational problem-solving approaches
Agency initiatives and program descriptions

Contributions should provide meaningful insights that other professionals can understand, evaluate, or potentially apply in their own organizations.

text:
EPCL uses a proposal-first submission process. Contributors initially submit a description of their proposed contribution rather than a completed manuscript.
This approach allows editors to evaluate the suitability of a proposed topic before contributors invest time developing a full manuscript.


STEP 01 — PROPOSAL



Select the appropriate journal and contribution category. Provide a proposed title and a description of the topic, purpose, and anticipated contribution.




STEP 02 — EDITORIAL REVIEW



Two editors assigned to the selected publication review the proposal. Editors consider its relevance, originality, potential contribution, and suitability for the publication.




STEP 03 — DECISION



Contributors receive notification of the editorial decision. Proposals may be approved, declined, or returned with a request for modification.
An approved proposal constitutes an invitation to develop a full manuscript. It does not guarantee publication.




STEP 04 — MANUSCRIPT DEVELOPMENT



Approved contributors receive instructions for developing their manuscripts, including the universal EPCL manuscript template and submission deadline.
The standard manuscript development period is 30 days following approval, subject to any extensions approved by the editorial team.




STEP 05 — MANUSCRIPT REVIEW



Submitted manuscripts undergo editorial review. Editors evaluate the quality, clarity, accuracy, relevance, and overall suitability of the manuscript.
Contributors may be asked to revise their work before a final decision is made.




STEP 06 — FINAL DECISION



Accepted manuscripts proceed to editorial preparation and publication. Contributors will be contacted regarding any necessary final revisions and publication details.

text:
Do I need to be a researcher or academic to submit?

No. EPCL welcomes contributions from practitioners, students, researchers, educators, administrators, and other professionals with relevant knowledge or experience.



Do I need to submit a completed article?

No. EPCL uses a proposal-first process. Initially, you submit a description of your proposed contribution. If approved, you will be invited to develop a full manuscript.



Does proposal approval guarantee publication?

No. Proposal approval is an invitation to develop a manuscript. The completed manuscript must still undergo editorial evaluation before a final publication decision.



Can I submit to more than one EPCL journal?

Contributors should submit proposals to the publication most closely aligned with their subject matter. If a proposed contribution could reasonably fit multiple publications, indicate this in the proposal description so the editorial team can consider its placement.



Can I submit if I have never published before?

Absolutely. EPCL encourages first-time contributors and welcomes individuals interested in sharing knowledge, research, and professional experience.



Will my manuscript undergo peer review?

EPCL uses an editorial review process involving assigned editors. The editorial team evaluates proposals and manuscripts for relevance, quality, accuracy, and suitability. The process should not be interpreted as external, independent scholarly peer review unless a particular publication explicitly identifies it as such.



Is there a submission fee?

There is currently no submission fee.

title: About the El Paso Crime Lab
text:
The Project
The El Paso Crime Lab is an independent public research project focused on crime, policing, and public safety in El Paso and the Borderland.
The project was established by Matthew Durán to make research and local public safety information more accessible to the public. It brings together academic research, publicly available data, statistical analysis, and other sources of evidence to examine issues affecting the region.
The El Paso Crime Lab is intended as a public-facing resource for research and information. Its purpose is not simply to present statistics, but to provide context, examine evidence, and help readers better understand the complex issues underlying crime and public safety.


The goal is simple: make rigorous research and local evidence easier to find, understand, and use.

title: About the El Paso Crime Lab
text:
Matthew Durán



Matthew Durán is a criminologist specializing in crime prevention, policing, and public safety research. He is a fourth-year PhD student in the School of Criminology and Criminal Justice at Arizona State University, where he teaches undergraduate and graduate courses on policing and research methods.
His research focuses on applying rigorous quantitative and experimental methods to understand crime patterns and evaluate criminal justice policies and interventions. His work spans policing, victimization, and crime prevention, with an emphasis on translating empirical research into useful insights for policy and practice.
Before beginning his doctoral training, Matthew worked in several criminal justice roles in the El Paso region, including as a crime analyst with the El Paso Police Department, a detention officer with the El Paso County Sheriff’s Office, and a licensed private investigator and fugitive recovery agent.
Matthew established the El Paso Crime Lab as a platform for sharing research, analysis, and public safety information related to El Paso and the broader Borderland.

title: About the El Paso Crime Lab
text:
Open Access

The El Paso Crime Lab is guided by a commitment to open access and public understanding.
Much of the information used in public safety decision-making is technical, difficult to access, or disconnected from the communities it concerns. This project seeks to make research and local data more accessible by presenting evidence in a clear and transparent way.
Where possible, data sources, methods, limitations, and supporting research are identified so that readers can examine the evidence for themselves.
The project is independent and does not represent or speak on behalf of any law enforcement agency or government organization.

title: Awards Program
text:
About the Awards
Public safety challenges require more than assumptions and conventional approaches. They require scientific inquiry, reliable data, thoughtful evaluation, and a willingness to continually improve policies and practices.
The EPCL Public Safety Science Awards recognize individuals throughout the El Paso–Borderland region who demonstrate these commitments through their professional work, research, education, or community contributions.
Whether conducting research, improving organizational data systems, evaluating programs, or helping translate scientific findings into practice, award recipients exemplify the importance of evidence-informed public safety.

title: Awards Program
text:
2026 Award Categories
The inaugural awards recognize contributions across six categories.


01. Dedication to Scientific Inquiry Award
Recognizes an individual who demonstrates exceptional dedication, initiative, and perseverance in pursuing scientific inquiry and advancing research-informed approaches to public safety.
This award recognizes curiosity, intellectual commitment, and the pursuit of scientific knowledge, including research proposals and projects that may still be in development.


02. Advancing Program Evaluation Award
Recognizes an individual who strengthens the ability to assess and improve programs through better data collection, measurement, evaluation systems, and organizational evaluation capacity.


03. Science in Action Award
Recognizes an individual who translates research, scientific knowledge, or data into practical improvements in public safety policies, programs, or practices.


04. Evidence-Based Practice Advancement Award
Recognizes an individual who promotes the use of scientific research and credible evidence in public safety policies, procedures, and practices.


05. Scientific Leadership Award
Recognizes an individual who demonstrates leadership in advancing scientific thinking, research collaboration, and evidence-informed decision-making within an organization or community.


06. Emerging Researcher Award
Recognizes a student or early-career professional demonstrating exceptional promise, initiative, or contribution to research and the science of public safety.

title: Awards Program
text:
Eligibility Requirements
To be considered for a 2026 EPCL Public Safety Science Award, nominees must meet the following requirements:

Geographic eligibility: Nominees must live, work, study, or conduct relevant professional or community activities within the El Paso–Borderland region.
2026 contributions: The work or contributions being recognized must have occurred between January 1 and December 31, 2026.
Individual recognition: Awards recognize individuals rather than organizations, agencies, or institutions.
Relevant contributions: Nominees must demonstrate contributions related to scientific inquiry, research, data, program evaluation, evidence-informed policy, or public safety practice.
Open professional eligibility: Students, researchers, analysts, public safety professionals, educators, administrators, program managers, and community members are welcome.

Formal research credentials, academic publications, and demonstrated program effectiveness are not required. Contributions may include foundational work such as improving data collection, developing measurement systems, establishing evaluation practices, or advancing research initiatives.

title: Awards Program
text:

Nominations are open to the public. Anyone may nominate an eligible individual, including nominating themselves.

Review the six award categories.
Select the category that best reflects the nominee’s contributions.

Describe the nominee’s work and provide an example of their contribution.

title: Comparing Alcohol-Related Traffic Fatalities Across Major Texas Cities
section: Is Drunk Driving Worse in El Paso?
text:
Is Drunk Driving Worse in El Paso?
A community facing a social problem such as drunk driving often wonders about it’s severity. Members of the community may ask, “Is it worse here than in other places?” To answer that question, we used three measurement strategies to assess the severity of loss of life from drunk driving. This report examines how El Paso compares to other large Texas cities in alcohol-related traffic fatalities between the years 2021 and 2025.
The findings show that:

118 people died in alcohol-related crashes in El Paso during the five-year period.
Roughly 1 out of every 3 traffic fatalities in El Paso involved alcohol.
Of the 30 large Texas cities, El Paso ranked:

5th highest in total alcohol-related fatalities
12th highest in per-capita rate
16th highest in the percentage of fatalities involving alcohol


Rather than focusing only on raw totals, this report compares cities using:

total counts,
per-capita rates, and
percentages of fatalities involving alcohol.

Together, these measures provide a clearer picture of how severe the problem is across communities of different sizes.














NoteKey Findings




El Paso recorded 118 alcohol-related traffic fatalities between 2021 and 2025.
Approximately 33.9% of all traffic fatalities in El Paso involved alcohol.
Of the 30 large Texas cities, El Paso ranked:

5th in total alcohol-related traffic fatalities
12th in per-capita rate
16th in percentage of all traffic fatalities involving alcohol

title: Protocol: A Scoping Review of Impaired Driving Research in El Paso, Texas
text:
Rationale for Study
Alcohol-related traffic deaths remain a persistent problem in the United States. While significant progress was achieved in the 1980s, such as the percentage of deaths involving a drunk driver falling from near 50% to around 30% by the year 2000, the problem has largely remained unchanged for over twenty-five years (National Highway Traffic Safety Administration 2023). Despite decades of legislative, enforcement, and public health efforts, driving while intoxicated continues to contribute substantially to motor vehicle crashes, injuries, and fatalities. Beyond its human toll, impaired driving imposes significant economic costs through healthcare expenditures, legal processing, and lost productivity (Baumberg 2006). These patterns highlight the need for continued evaluation of how impaired driving is measured, addressed, and prevented.
Much of the existing research on impaired driving relies on national or multi-state analyses, which are valuable for identifying broad trends and evaluating large-scale policy interventions but may be less applicable for individual communities. Moreover, a substantial portion of foundational empirical work in this area was conducted in the late 1980s and early 2000s, reflecting policy environments and enforcement strategies that may differ meaningfully from contemporary conditions (e.g., (Elder et al. 2004; Wagenaar et al. 1995)). Consequently, findings derived from national samples may obscure important local variation and may not generalize to specific communities. This limitation is particularly salient for policymakers and practitioners who must make decisions within the constraints and realities of their own jurisdictions.
A jurisdiction-specific approach offers an opportunity to examine impaired driving within its full local context. For example, in a setting such as El Paso, impaired driving patterns may be shaped by unique demographic characteristics, cross-border dynamics, transportation infrastructure, and localized enforcement strategies. These contextual factors are critical for interpreting trends and evaluating interventions but are frequently overlooked in broader analyses. At the same time, the body of evidence within a single jurisdiction is often fragmented. Relevant information may exist across peer-reviewed studies, government reports, and program evaluations, each using different definitions, measures, and methodological approaches. This fragmentation can lead to inconsistent conclusions, and missed opportunities for coordinated policy responses. Without a comprehensive synthesis, stakeholders may lack a clear understanding of how different components of the system interact or where critical gaps in knowledge remain.

title: Protocol: A Scoping Review of Impaired Driving Research in El Paso, Texas
text:
Objectives
The objective of this review is to systematically map and synthesize the full range of available evidence on impaired driving within the El Paso region. Consistent with scoping review methodology,1 the aim is not to evaluate intervention effectiveness, but rather to characterize the nature, extent, and distribution of existing evidence across multiple domains. Specifically, this review will integrate findings from both peer-reviewed and non-peer reviewed literature to develop a comprehensive understanding of how impaired driving is studied and documented within the jurisdiction.
1 This review will follow the reporting guidelines outlined in the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). https://www.prisma-statement.org/scopingThe review will meet the following objectives:

Describe how impaired driving is measured and reported across studies, including indicators of prevalence such as arrests, crashes, injuries, and fatalities;
Map the range of documented risk factors associated with impaired driving;
Catalog and describe the types of interventions, enforcement strategies, and policy approaches that have been implemented and evaluated; and
Identify gaps, inconsistencies, and areas of fragmentation in the existing evidence base.

By organizing the literature across these domains, the review aims to provide a structured overview of how impaired driving is conceptualized, measured, and addressed within the local context. In doing so, this study will provide a foundational evidence map to support future research, data integration efforts, and policy development at the local level, moving beyond fragmented and generalized national findings toward a more context-specific understanding of impaired driving dynamics within the jurisdiction.

title: Protocol: A Scoping Review of Impaired Driving Research in El Paso, Texas
section: Criteria for Inclusion and Exclusion of Studies
text:
Criteria for Inclusion and Exclusion of Studies

Definition
Eligible studies must focus on the topic of impaired driving. In line with prior research, this review defines impaired driving as driving under the influence of drug or alcohol (Rezapour and Ksaibati 2022). Studies that assess a form of impaired driving outside of this definition will be excluded (e.g., driver fatigue).


Study Design
Any empirical study design will be considered, including observational/descriptive studies, qualitative designs, quasi-experimental evaluations, time series analyses, and program or policy evaluations. Both peer-reviewed literature and gray literature, such as government reports and agency publications, will be included to capture the full scope of available evidence. Studies must be available in English or Spanish and include data from the year 2000 onward. Studies will be excluded if they consist solely of editorials, commentaries, or conceptual discussions without empirical data.


Location
Eligible studies must use data specific to El Paso, Texas or a clearly identifiable subset of that jurisdiction.

text:
Synthesis of Results
The synthesis of results will focus on descriptive and thematic analysis. Findings will be organized into primary domains, such as prevalence, risk factors, and intervention evaluations. Within each domain, studies will be grouped based on outcome type, data source, and methodological approach. Results will be presented using narrative synthesis supported by summary tables. Consistent with scoping review methodology, a formal critical appraisal of study quality or risk of bias will not be required. However, relevant limitations and data quality considerations will be noted and incorporated into the interpretation of findings.
